q: What does the Elvis operator ?: do in Kotlin?
a: It safely calls a method on a nullable receiver and returns null if it was nil
It throws an exception on null
It returns the left operand if non-null, else the right one
It compares two values for equality
e: val name = input ?: "default" — if input is null, "default" is used. Handy for defaults and early returns.

q: launch vs async in coroutines — the difference?
a: launch is fully synchronous and blocks, while async runs the work on a new thread
launch returns a Job; async returns a Deferred result you await
async can't be cancelled
There is no difference
e: launch is for work without a return value (fire-and-forget). async starts a computation whose result you get via .await() — great for parallel requests.

e: val is a read-only reference and can't be reassigned. Use var for a mutable variable.

q: Why is data lost on screen rotation, and how do you keep it?
a: The OS clears the heap on rotation, so you must serialize everything to disk first
The Activity is recreated; use a ViewModel or onSaveInstanceState
It's a bug; wrap it in try/catch
Disable rotation permanently
e: Rotation is a config change → Activity destroy/recreate. A ViewModel survives recreation; use onSaveInstanceState (Bundle) for small data.

q: What is lateinit var for?
a: To schedule a property's initializer to run on a background dispatcher later
To make a property nullable
To declare a non-null property and assign it later (e.g. in onCreate)
To create a lazy property
e: lateinit defers init of a non-null var. Accessing it before assignment throws UninitializedPropertyAccessException. Not for primitives or val.

q: Why use viewModelScope for coroutines in a ViewModel?
a: It pins every coroutine to the main thread and caches their results between rotations
They are auto-cancelled when the ViewModel is cleared — no leaks
It makes coroutines faster
It retries failed coroutines automatically
e: viewModelScope is tied to the ViewModel lifecycle: on onCleared() all its coroutines are cancelled, preventing leaks and wasted work.

q: Where is a sealed class especially useful?
a: For closed state hierarchies (Loading/Success/Error) with an exhaustive when
To create singletons
To replace interfaces
Only for defining a fixed set of enum-like integer constants shared across modules
e: sealed restricts subclasses to one module. A when over a sealed type is checked for completeness — add a state, forget to handle it, get an error.

q: StateFlow vs a plain Flow — the difference?
a: A plain Flow holds the latest value while StateFlow re-runs its block per collector
StateFlow is hot, holds a current value, and replays it to new collectors
StateFlow can't be collected
StateFlow only works in the background
e: A plain Flow is cold (restarts per collector). StateFlow is hot, has .value, and emits the latest value to new subscribers — like LiveData.

q: What is the ViewModel responsible for in MVVM?
a: Directly drawing UI widgets and handling their click and touch listeners itself
Holding UI state without referencing the View, surviving its recreation
Managing files on disk
Running database migrations
e: The ViewModel holds UI state and presentation logic and exposes it via LiveData/StateFlow. It keeps no View reference — hence testability and rotation survival.

q: A suspend Retrofit call — which dispatcher should you run it on?
a: Always wrap it manually in withContext(Dispatchers.IO) or it will block the UI
Retrofit moves off the main thread itself; calling from Main is fine
Only Dispatchers.Default
Only a new Thread
e: Modern Retrofit with suspend functions does IO in the background (enqueue). So calling it from viewModelScope (Main) is safe, no manual withContext(IO).

q: apply vs also — the difference?
a: apply: receiver this, returns object; also: receiver it, returns object
They are identical
apply returns Unit
also returns the lambda's result while apply returns the receiver object itself
e: Both return the object itself. apply suits configuration (this.field = ...), also suits side effects with it (logging, validation).

q: Classic cause of a memory leak on Android?
a: Declaring too many data classes, since each generates equals, hashCode and copy
A long-lived object holding an Activity Context (static, singleton, stray thread)
Using val instead of var
Launching many coroutines in viewModelScope without ever cancelling the parent job
e: If a singleton/static/anonymous thread holds an Activity Context, GC can't collect it after destruction. Use applicationContext or weak references.

q: Why mark a function inline?
a: The compiler caches its return value so repeated calls with same args are skipped
Its body and lambdas are inlined at the call site, avoiding lambda overhead
To make it private
To run it asynchronously
e: inline on a higher-order function avoids allocating Function objects and enables non-local return and reified types. Overuse bloats bytecode.

q: What is recomposition in Jetpack Compose?
a: Re-invoking Composable functions when observed state changes, to update the UI
Rebuilding and recompiling the whole project whenever any Composable state changes
Clearing memory
Restarting the entire app
e: Compose is declarative: when state (e.g. MutableState) changes, the affected Composables are re-invoked, updating only the necessary UI parts.

q: SupervisorJob vs a regular Job — the point?
a: One child failing doesn't cancel its siblings or the parent scope
With it, cancelling any child cancels all the others in the same scope
It makes coroutines synchronous
It forbids cancellation
e: With a regular Job a child's failure cancels the parent and siblings. SupervisorJob isolates failures — other coroutines keep running. Good for independent tasks.

q: What is a companion object in Kotlin?
a: An object bound to a class giving member access without an instance (static-like)
A nested class that holds per-instance mutable state for its outer class
A default interface
A special declaration used to create and launch a new coroutine scoped to the class
e: Kotlin has no static. A companion object inside a class holds class-level members (factories, constants), accessed as ClassName.member.

q: What's special about a suspend function?
a: It can pause without blocking the thread and resume later
It always starts a brand new thread for every call you make to it
It can't return a value
It blocks the thread until done
e: suspend marks a suspension point. The compiler turns the function into a state machine; the thread is freed while waiting instead of blocking.
